parts.title: The Nest
parts.summary: Aisle twenty-two is empty, but camera six still shows the man sitting there. Marcus finds a nest on the top shelf, with a notebook tracking all three of their shifts and Dana's alarm code. Camera six's clock is frozen at 4:37: someone looped the feed. Then the generator dies two days early, the fuel can is empty and still wet, and a voice behind you in the dark says not to open the bay door. Nobody's there.
script: Aisle twenty-two is empty. But on Dana's screen, he's still sitting there.
Your radio crackles. "He's right in front of you," Dana says. "He hasn't moved."
You're standing on the exact spot. Nothing but crumbs and a torn bag.
Marcus looks up. On the top shelf, twenty feet up, a sleeping bag hangs over the edge.
He climbs. "Somebody's been living up here," Marcus says. "For weeks."
Canned food. A flashlight. Store hoodies with the tags still on.
And a notebook. He drops it down to you.
Inside are three columns. Dana. Marcus. And a drawing of your orange beanie.
Every shift you've worked since October. Under Dana's name, four numbers. "That's my alarm code," she whispers.
Back at the office, camera six still shows him. Same spot. Same bag.
Dana leans in. The clock in the corner of the feed isn't moving. Four thirty-seven. Frozen.
"Someone looped it," Marcus says. "We've been watching a recording."
Then the generator coughs twice, and the whole store goes black.
"That's two days early," Dana says. "Somebody drained it."
Your flashlight finds the fuel can. Tipped over. Empty. Still wet.
Whoever did it was here a minute ago. And they're still inside.
Then a voice, right behind you in the dark. "Don't open the bay door."
You spin around. Your light hits the racking. Nobody's there.

parts.title: Ray
parts.summary: You spring the trap in aisle twenty-two and catch the stowaway: Ray. He confesses to living in the nest since October, looping camera six, and draining the generator so the lights wouldn't betray them from the road. Midway, he drops the real bomb — he used to work here, knew Dana before she was manager. At two in the morning, three heavy knocks hammer the buried bay door. Ray whispers the truck crew has arrived.

end_card.title: PART 4
end_card.hook: Who is prying the bay door open?

script: The stowaway drops from the ceiling into your arms.
You and Marcus wait in pitch black, flashlights killed.
Dana stares at the monitor. Camera six still loops the empty nest.
A shadow falls. Marcus snags him mid-drop. "Got you, bastard."
The man gasps, hood yanked back. Gray-green fabric, days of stubble.
"Ray," Dana's voice cracks over the radio. "His name is Ray."
You cinch zip ties on his wrists. He doesn't flinch.
"The lights could be seen from the road," he says. "Had to kill them."
"From who?" you ask. He clamps his mouth shut.
Dana's beam finds the notebook. "You knew my alarm code."
Ray smiles, exhausted. "I used to work here. Before you."
"Day manager, twenty nineteen," he says. "I stocked nights. You yelled at me for stacking apples wrong."
Dana goes pale. "You're the one who vanished."
"Didn't vanish. Got evicted. Came back to the only roof I knew."
The wall clock clicks past two in the morning.
Three slow knocks hammer the buried bay door.
Metal screams. The door shudders upward an inch.
Ray's eyes lock on yours. "They found us."

parts.title: Morning
parts.summary: The truck crew forces the bay door. Ray explains he overheard them before the storm. The keypad beeps with Dana's code; the page is torn from Ray's notebook. Ray, cut loose, leads them through his crawlspace and the roof hatch; outside, they haul the bay door down and lock the crew in with their own tow chain. Marcus is missing: he's inside with the crew, the torn page in his pocket. At dawn, police arrive; Dana credits Ray; the front doors finally open.
script: The bay door screams up another inch. Headlights spill through the gap.
"Who is that?" Dana snaps at Ray. "Who did you tell?"
"Nobody," Ray says. "I heard them in the lot before the storm. They want to empty this place while the roads are closed."
Through the gap, a yellow plow truck idles in the snow. Men in headlamps are digging.
"Barricade," Dana says. "Now."
Marcus fires up the forklift. You drag pallets of water against the door.
Then the keypad by the bay door beeps. Once. Twice.
Green light. Someone outside just typed Dana's alarm code.
Dana grabs Ray's notebook and flips to the back. The page with her code is torn out.
"I never took it," Ray says. "I swear."
The pallets start sliding. The door rises a foot. A gloved hand reaches under.
"Is there another way out?" you shout.
Ray looks up. "Roof hatch. Cut me loose."
Dana stares at him for one long second. Then she nods, and you cut his zip ties.
Ray climbs the racking in aisle twenty-two, and you all follow him into the dark.
Above the top shelf, there's a crawlspace only he knows. It runs right over the loading dock.
Below you, four men in headlamps squeeze under the bay door.
Ray pops the roof hatch. Snow pours in.
You slide down the drift to the dock, right next to their truck. It's still running.
You and Ray haul the bay door down. Dana wraps the plow's tow chain through the handles and snaps the lock.
Inside, fists hammer the door. They're trapped in the dock.
Then you notice Marcus isn't with you.
Through the crack under the door, you see his yellow vest. He's inside with them. Talking.
A torn notebook page sticks out of his vest pocket.
Dana's voice cracks. "Marcus had my code."
Ray stares at the door. "He's the one I saw in the lot."
By dawn, the snow stops. Red and blue lights flash at the top of the drift.
A county plow clears the lot, and three police cruisers roll in behind it.
They unchain the bay door. Four men come out in handcuffs. Then Marcus, who won't look at Dana.
An officer asks who caught them. Dana points at Ray. "He did."
Behind you, the front doors finally slide all the way open.

parts.title: Wake Up
parts.summary: You doze off on the train home and wake somewhere wrong: a silent car of passengers hidden behind newspapers, a phone stuck at 2:14, black windows, stops you've never heard of. An old woman is horrified to see you; she doesn't know where you are either. She introduces herself as June, talks with you, notices your stop isn't on the map, and gives you nine handwritten rules. The conductor punches tickets; a man in a red tracksuit nearly talks back and June saves him. June's own ticket is punched like lace. Then the man in red mocks the passengers, they copy him, he won't freeze, the lights go out, and he's gone. On the front page of a newspaper where he stood is a man in a red tracksuit.
script: You finally catch the train home after a long day. All you want is your bed.
The second you sit down, the fatigue hits. A small nap couldn't hurt.
If only you knew how wrong you'd be.
You wake up to silence. Just the clack of the tracks.
Every passenger hides behind a newspaper. Nobody moves.
Two fourteen in the morning. No signal.
The route map lists stops you've never heard of.
Across the aisle, an old woman knits a scarf so long it trails across the floor.
She's the only one not reading. She's watching you.
When your eyes meet, her face falls.
"Oh no," she whispers. "Not another one."
"Where are we?" you ask.
"I'm not sure, sweetheart. I wish I knew."
She sits down beside you. "I'm June. Fell asleep too?"
You nod. "Long day." "They always are," June says.
"Where were you headed?" she asks. "Elm Street."
June glances at the map. Elm Street isn't on it.
"Okay," June says quietly. "Then listen to me carefully."
She presses a folded sheet into your hands. "Do exactly what it says."
Rule one. Do not make eye contact with the other passengers.
Rule two. When the conductor asks for your ticket, smile. Do not speak.
Rule three. If the lights go out, keep your eyes closed until the doors chime.
Rule four. Never go into the last car.
Rule five. If someone calls your name, it isn't them.
Rule six. Your stop is the one that shows your name. Get off, no matter what's on the platform.
Rule seven. Do not fall asleep again.
Rule eight. If your reflection blinks before you do, look away.
Rule nine. If the passengers start copying you, freeze.
Then, from the end of the car: click. Click.
A tall conductor comes down the aisle, punching tickets. His cap hides his eyes. Not his smile.
A man in a red tracksuit films him. "Bro, is this a prank show?"
"Ticket, please." The man starts to argue. June kicks his shoe, hard.
He blinks, then grins. Click. The conductor moves on.
Then he's at your seat. "Ticket, please."
In your pocket is a ticket you never bought. You smile. Click.
June stares at the hole, then holds up her own ticket. It's punched so many times it looks like lace.
"One hole," she whispers, "for every stop you miss."
"Watch this," the man in red laughs, and waves at the passengers.
Every newspaper drops. Every hand in the car waves back.
"Freeze," June hisses. You go still. He doesn't.
He stands and bows. They all stand and bow. He laughs. They laugh, silently.
Then every passenger takes one step toward him.
The lights go out.
When the lights flicker on, his seat is empty.
On the floor lies a newspaper. Front page: a man in a red tracksuit.

parts.title: The Last Car
parts.summary: The man in red is on the front page of a newspaper dated November 3, 1987, and so is every paper in the car. June won't say where he went; her eyes go to the last car, where a single handle swings. His phone starts ringing in there, and June holds you down: never the last car. The lights go out; eyes shut; the conductor's punch clicks closer until it's beside your ear and something waits for you to look. You don't. The doors chime, and for the first time every passenger has turned a page. Then your phone rings with no signal: Mom. June begs you not to. You answer, and in your mother's voice it says your name: "I'm waiting at the next stop. Get off the train."
script: You woke up on a night train with a list of rules. One passenger broke a rule, and now he's gone.
The man in red smiles up at you from the front page.
You pick it up. The paper is soft and yellow, like it's been lying there for years.
The date under the headline is nineteen eighty seven. November third.
You look down the car. Every newspaper has the same date.
June doesn't look up from her knitting. "Put it down, sweetheart."
"Where did he go?" you ask.
June's needles stop. Her eyes go to the door at the end of the car.
Through its little window, the last car is dark. One handle swings back and forth.
"He's not in there," June says. "Not anymore."
Then, from the last car, a phone starts ringing.
His ringtone. It rings and rings. Nobody turns a page.
Without meaning to, you start to stand.
June's hand clamps onto your knee. "Never the last car. Never."
The ringing stops.
Above you, the lights flicker.
June squeezes your hand. "Eyes shut, sweetheart. Now."
The lights go out. You squeeze your eyes shut.
In the dark, only the clack of the tracks.
Then, from the end of the car: click.
Click. Closer.
Click. Right beside your ear.
You can feel someone bending over you, waiting for you to look.
You don't look.
The doors chime.
The lights are back. June lets out a long breath. "Good. That was good."
Your hands are shaking. "June, what was that?" you whisper.
She picks her knitting back up. "The conductor. In the dark, he looks for anyone with their eyes open."
"And if I had looked?" June doesn't answer.
Then you notice the passengers.
For the first time, every one of them has turned a page.
In your pocket, your phone buzzes.
Still no signal. But someone is calling.
It's your mom.
June goes very still. "Don't, sweetheart."
But it's your mom. Your thumb is already on the green button.
"Mom?"
Nothing. Then, very softly, in her voice, it says your name.
"I'm waiting at the next stop. Get off the train."

parts.title: Your Stop
parts.summary: June ends the call: rule five, it isn't them. She shows her lace-punched ticket: her stop was November 3, 1987, her mother waited on the platform smiling too wide, and she stayed on, and has stayed on ever since. But rule six says get off at your stop no matter what is on the platform, and the rules are in your own handwriting. Your reflection keeps reading after you look up, then blinks; you look away (rule eight). The route map scrambles into your name, the train stops, and your mom is on the platform, smiling too wide. June begs you to stay; the rules say go. The lamp flickers and she is one step closer.
script: It's still talking. "Get off at the next stop, honey. I'm right here."
June pulls the phone from your ear and ends the call.
"Rule five," she says. "If someone calls your name, it isn't them."
Your hands won't stop shaking. "It sounded exactly like her."
"They always do." June picks her knitting back up, but her needles keep missing.
"How do you know all this?" you ask.
June is quiet for a long time. Then she holds up her ticket, punched so many times it looks like lace.
"November third, nineteen eighty seven. That was my stop."
"My mother was waiting on the platform, waving. Smiling too wide."
"So I stayed on." She looks down at her ticket. "I've stayed on ever since."
You unfold the rules sheet again.
Rule six. Your stop is the one that shows your name on the map. Get off, no matter what is on the platform.
"June, the rules say you should have gotten off."
Her needles stop. She doesn't look at you.
Then you notice the handwriting.
The loops on the g's. The little line through the sevens.
It's your handwriting. Yours.
"I didn't write this," you whisper. "I've never seen this before."
In the black window, your reflection is still looking down at the page.
You're already looking up. It isn't.
Then your reflection lifts its head. And blinks.
You look away so fast your neck cracks.
"Rule eight," June whispers. "Good. Don't look back at it."
Above the doors, the route map flickers.
The name of the next stop scrambles, letter by letter.
Then it spells your name.
The brakes start to squeal. The train is slowing down.
June grabs your wrist. "Don't get off. Look at what's waiting."
The doors chime and slide open.
It's your mom, standing on the platform in her work coat, waving.
She is smiling. Too wide.
June's grip tightens. "It isn't her, sweetheart. It never is."
But the rules, in your handwriting, say get off, no matter what is on the platform.
Behind your mom, the platform lamp flickers off.
When it comes back on, she's one step closer to the doors.

parts.title: Get Off
parts.summary: The thing wearing your mom waits at the open doors. June begs you to stay. She admits you wrote the rules yourself, every ride, and every time you stayed with her. Your ticket has one hole; hers is lace. You pull free, step off, and walk past the thing without looking while it whispers your name in three voices. June mouths 'Go' as the train leaves. At dawn your phone has signal and twenty-three missed calls from your real mom. You got off. In your pocket, under rule nine, a line you don't remember writing: Rule ten. Come back for June.
script: The lamp flickers again. Your mom is at the edge of the platform now, close enough to touch the doors.
"Sweetheart, come here," she says. Her mouth doesn't move with the words.
June's nails dig into your wrist. "Stay. Please. That's how it gets you."
You look down at the rules in your other hand. Your handwriting. Rule six.
"June," you say. "Who wrote these?"
June's eyes fill with tears. "You did. Every time."
"Every time you ride, you write them down. And every time, you stay with me."
You think of her ticket, punched so many times it looks like lace.
Then you look at yours. One hole.
"How many times have I been on this train?"
June doesn't answer. She just holds on tighter.
The doors chime. They're about to close.
You pull your wrist free. "I'm sorry, June."
You step through the doors.
The cold hits you first. The platform smells like rain and rust.
Your mom is right in front of you. Up close, her smile goes all the way back to her ears.
Rule six. No matter what is on the platform.
You walk past her. You don't look.
Behind you, something whispers your name in her voice. Then in June's. Then in yours.
You keep walking.
The doors hiss shut behind you.
You turn around once.
June is at the window, holding up her lace ticket. Her lips make one word: "Go."
The train pulls away into the dark. The platform is empty.
Your phone buzzes. Full signal. Five fifty-two in the morning.
Twenty-three missed calls. All from Mom. The real one.
You call her back, and she picks up crying. "Where are you?"
"I missed my stop," you say. "But I got off."
The rules are still in your pocket, folded up, in your handwriting.
You read them one last time. Then you drop them in the trash by the stairs.
You walk home as the sun comes up.
You never take the night train again.
